options: Stop the burning, then a primary survey led by the airway, with oxygen after smoke
Size the burn by the rule of nines before anything else, since fluids depend on it
Cool the burns under running water first, then start the primary survey
Peel off the melted clothing stuck to the skin first, then cover the burns and assess
nodes.chainStep: Stop the burning: remove burning or hot items, clothing, belts and jewelry, leaving melted or stuck clothing to experienced staff; primary survey as for any trauma patient, airway first; 100% oxygen after smoke or with facial burns; major burn: two large-bore IV lines, through unburned skin if possible; ask about an enclosed space, a fall, blast or jump, and any fluid given en route
nodes.why: Every burn patient is a trauma patient first: airway, breathing and circulation come before the burn, and the burn is sized after the primary and secondary surveys. The first step of burn care is still to stop the burning, by removing hot and burning items, clothing and jewelry, because burned areas swell; clothing that has melted onto or stuck to the wound is left to experienced staff. Cooling matters but does not come before the airway. Oxygen goes to anyone exposed to smoke or with facial burns, for carbon monoxide or cyanide. The history asks about an enclosed space (inhalation injury), an explosion or a jump (other injuries), and any fluid given on the way in.

orders.dose: Remove burning and hot items, clothing, belts and jewelry; leave melted or firmly stuck clothing to experienced staff
Make the scene safe first: switch off any current, gloves for chemicals

Major burn: two large-bore peripheral lines, preferably through unburned skin (through burned skin if needed); central or intraosseous access if peripheral access fails
Ask the volume and type; it counts toward the first 8 hours

The skin burns do not measure it; electrolytes, creatinine, CK and a urinalysis for myoglobin

Thermal burn, ABCs holding; no smoke signs, injury, current or chemical
Not heat, current or chemical; frostbite, radiation or friction

nodes.ask: Burned airway at risk: stridor, hoarseness, or deep facial or mouth burns. Next?
options: Intubate early, before the swelling closes the airway, with a difficult airway plan
Nebulized epinephrine and IV dexamethasone first, intubating if the stridor worsens
High-flow oxygen by mask, with a repeat airway check in an hour
Bronchoscopy first, to prove an inhalation injury before placing a tube
nodes.chainStep: Early intubation with a difficult airway plan (fiberoptic intubation for supraglottic swelling), before the edema closes the airway; secure the tube firmly; semi-upright if stable; COHb and lactate on a blood gas
nodes.why: Hoarseness, stridor, accessory muscle use, deep facial burns, burns inside the mouth, swelling or trouble swallowing are indications for early intubation. Burn edema progresses over the first 24 hours, fluid creep adds to it, and stridor appears only once the airway is already critically narrow, so the decision is made before the swelling; if there is any doubt, it is safer to intubate. A swollen supraglottis makes laryngoscopy hard, so a fiberoptic approach that keeps spontaneous breathing is the accepted safe route. Steroids, inhaled or IV, are not proven to help, and waiting for a bronchoscopy or a later check risks losing the airway.

orders.dose: Hoarseness, stridor, accessory muscle use or sternal retraction; extensive deep facial burns; burns inside the mouth; significant edema or risk of it; trouble swallowing; failing to clear secretions, tiring, or poor oxygenation or ventilation; reduced consciousness with impaired airway reflexes; a burn over 40 to 50% TBSA; a transfer with an airway issue and no one to intubate en route
Fiberoptic intubation for supraglottic swelling; ketamine preserves hemodynamic stability
Succinylcholine can be used in the acute burn but is avoided from about 24 to 48 hours (hyperkalemia); rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg gives reasonable conditions after a major burn
Inhaled or IV: not proven beneficial
Fix it very securely; keep the patient semi-upright if hemodynamically stable

nodes.label: Blood gas after the airway is secured

outcomes.if: COHb or lactate raised; carbon monoxide or cyanide likely
COHb and lactate normal, skin burned; airway secured

orders.dose: Does not exclude inhalation injury: on 100% oxygen the COHb falls within hours, so a level taken several hours after the injury can be low

outcomes.if: COHb and lactate normal, no skin burn; airway secured

nodes.ask: Soot or singed nasal hair after a fire; voice, breathing and pressure normal. Next?
options: 100% oxygen, a COHb, and a look at the larynx, repeated as the swelling evolves
Intubate now, since singed nasal hair confirms that an inhalation injury is present
Room air with pulse oximetry, as a normal saturation excludes carbon monoxide
A chest film, as a clear film rules out an inhalation injury at this stage
nodes.chainStep: 100% oxygen; COHb on a blood gas; direct or fiberoptic laryngoscopy for edema, repeated as edema progresses over 24 hours; semi-upright; intubate if swelling, hoarseness or stridor appears
nodes.why: Soot shows smoke exposure but on its own does not diagnose an inhalation injury or its severity, and facial burns, carbonaceous sputum and singed nasal hair predict airway swelling poorly. Hot smoke without facial burns can be watched closely if there is no severe upper airway edema. A direct or fiberoptic look at the larynx is quick and can avoid an unneeded tube, and because edema progresses over 24 hours the look is repeated. Pulse oximetry can read falsely high with carbon monoxide, so the COHb comes from a blood gas, and chest films are often normal early.

orders.dose: Direct or fiberoptic laryngoscopy for edema, redness or ulceration; repeated, as edema progresses over 24 hours
100% oxygen; COHb on a blood gas, as pulse oximetry may read falsely high
Semi-upright if hemodynamically stable
Onset can be delayed; warn the patient
ABLS omits soot and singed hair; the Denver criteria add suspected smoke inhalation and singed facial hair
orders.note: StatPearls facial burns gives both; the key follows ABLS and repeats the look.

sources.where: Diagnosis: upper and lower airway damage; Treatment: airway

outcomes.if: Airway swelling; edema on the scope, or hoarseness or stridor develops
COHb raised, airway clear; no edema on the scope, voice normal
Airway clear, COHb normal, skin burned; no edema on the scope
Smoke only, airway clear, COHb normal; no edema, no skin burn

nodes.summary: Smoke without a skin burn, COHb and lactate normal: symptoms can be delayed and airway edema progresses over 24 hours, so keep the patient semi-upright, repeat the look at the larynx, intubate at the first edema, hoarseness or stridor, and warn about delayed symptoms before any discharge. A patient already intubated keeps the tube very securely fixed and stays semi-upright. No steroids, no prophylactic antibiotics.

Smoke with confusion, low pressure, or a raised COHb or lactate: carbon monoxide and cyanide come first; pulse oximetry can read falsely normal, so the COHb is measured on a blood gas. Soot with confusion, coma, seizures, slow breathing, shock or a metabolic acidosis continues in the toxicology pathway (pw_tox) for hydroxocobalamin without waiting for a cyanide level. An alert patient with a raised COHb continues in the headache pathway (pw_headache) for 100% oxygen and the hyperbaric criteria. The larynx is examined as after any smoke, and the burn is then cooled, sized and resuscitated as in this pathway, with fluids timed from the burn.

Burns with other injuries: the trauma primary survey comes first in the major trauma pathway (pw_trauma), because life threats from the injury or the airway take priority over transfer to a burn center. Stop the burning and give oxygen meanwhile, and do not let the visible burn distract from less obvious injuries. The burn is sized at the secondary survey, fluids are timed from the burn, and burns with concomitant trauma meet the burn center criteria. After closed-space smoke, the COHb is measured and cyanide considered as in pw_tox.

Electrical or lightning injury: continue in the environmental injury pathway (pw_environmental) for the ECG, monitoring, admission and myoglobinuria fluids titrated to the urine output. Current damages deep tissue under small or absent burns, so the CK, urine and compartments are checked. Contact burns are covered, not routinely cooled; any skin burn is sized as here, knowing the size understates the injury. Electrical burns meet the burn center criteria.

nodes.ask: Burned, hypotensive on arrival, no smoke or injury yet seen. Next?
options: Treat it as shock from another cause and search for it: bleeding, chest, cord
Burn shock from the capillary leak: double the formula rate until the pressure recovers
Start norepinephrine for burn vasoplegia, then size the burn
Cool the burns and give the first 8 hours of the formula as a bolus
nodes.chainStep: Hypotension soon after a burn: resuscitate and search for another cause (hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, neurogenic shock, abdominal or pelvic bleeding) by the trauma pathway; cyanide after closed-space smoke
nodes.why: Hypotension is often a late finding in burn shock, so a burned patient who arrives hypotensive has another cause until shown otherwise: hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, neurogenic shock, or abdominal and pelvic bleeding. The visible burn must not distract from injuries that are less apparent. Extra burn fluid or a vasopressor does not find the cause, and boluses beyond need worsen the burn edema.

orders.dose: Hemothorax, cardiac tamponade, neurogenic shock, internal abdominal and pelvic bleeding
Airway, hemorrhage control and the trauma survey; do not let the visible burn hide other injuries

nodes.summary: Hypotension soon after a burn is not burn shock until other causes are excluded: continue in the major trauma pathway (pw_trauma) for hemothorax, tamponade, neurogenic shock and abdominal or pelvic bleeding; after closed-space smoke, cyanide is a cause of low pressure (pw_tox). Once the cause is treated, the burn is sized here and fluids are timed from the burn.

nodes.ask: Chemical on the skin, eyes spared, clothing still on. First?
options: Gloves, clothing off, brush off any dry powder, then a long running-water rinse
Neutralize it on the skin: a weak acid for an alkali, or bicarbonate for an acid
Pour water over the dry powder at once, then brush off what is left
Cover with a dry dressing and give the antidote before rinsing
nodes.chainStep: Barrier protection for staff; remove and bag contaminated clothing; brush off dry powder or solid chemical; irrigate with running water for 30 minutes to 2 hours; no neutralizing agents; an eye splash is irrigated first (pw_eye)
nodes.why: Contaminated clothing comes off first, with barrier protection for staff. Dried alkali or other solid chemical is brushed away before rinsing, and then the skin is irrigated with plenty of running water, for 30 minutes to 2 hours by the Burns Trauma consensus. Neutralizing agents are not used: no study shows them better than water, and the reaction releases heat that can add injury. Even hydrofluoric acid is irrigated first; its calcium gluconate comes after the rinse. A chemical in the eye goes first, to irrigation at once.

orders.dose: Remove contaminated clothing; brush dried alkali or solid chemical away first, then rinse
Running water as soon as possible, for 30 minutes to 2 hours
Not used routinely: the reaction releases heat and can add injury
Barrier protection; contaminated clothing removed and contained

sources.where: First aid: what not to do

orders.dose: Copious irrigation at once; the red eye pathway (pw_eye) sets the end point

outcomes.if: Hydrofluoric acid; pain out of proportion, a rust or wheel cleaner
Another acid or alkali; no hydrofluoric acid

nodes.ask: Hydrofluoric acid on the fingers, irrigated; pain out of proportion to the burn. Next?
options: Calcium gluconate gel massaged in, with calcium, magnesium and an ECG
Bicarbonate soaks to neutralize the acid, with a dry dressing
Silver sulfadiazine dressing with a wound check in 48 hours
IV opioid titrated to the pain, with the hand elevated and splinted high
nodes.chainStep: 2.5% calcium gluconate gel massaged in for 15 to 30 minutes, reapplied every 10 to 15 minutes until the pain eases; subcutaneous 5% calcium gluconate if pain persists; calcium, magnesium, potassium, bicarbonate and kidney function; ECG and monitoring
nodes.why: Pain far beyond the look of the wound is the hallmark of hydrofluoric acid. Irrigation dilutes the acid but does not bind fluoride already in the tissue, so calcium gluconate is the cornerstone: 2.5% gel massaged in, then subcutaneous 5% calcium gluconate if the pain persists, with relief of pain as the sign that it works. Even a skin burn can lower calcium and magnesium and raise potassium, with QT prolongation and arrhythmias, so the electrolytes are checked and the heart is monitored. Neutralizing soaks are not recommended for chemical burns, a dressing leaves the fluoride in the tissue untreated, and an opioid treats the pain, not the fluoride.

orders.dose: 2.5% gel applied liberally and massaged in for 15 to 30 minutes; reapplied every 10 to 15 minutes until the pain improves
5% calcium gluconate infiltrated at 0.5 mL per cm2, slightly beyond the visible margins; in the digits at most 0.5 mL per phalanx
Calcium, magnesium, potassium, bicarbonate and kidney function; ECG and continuous monitoring in moderate or severe exposures
Over 5% TBSA (over 1% if the acid is above 50%), inhalation, ingestion or abnormal electrolytes: continuous cardiac monitoring and serial labs; IV calcium for hypocalcemia
Amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide are relatively contraindicated; correct the electrolytes

sources.where: History and Physical; Evaluation; Treatment / Management

nodes.summary: Hydrofluoric acid burn: irrigation, then 2.5% calcium gluconate gel until the pain settles, subcutaneous 5% calcium gluconate if it does not, and calcium, magnesium and potassium with an ECG. Admission with continuous monitoring for a burn over 5% TBSA (over 1% with acid above 50%) or any electrolyte change, with IV calcium for hypocalcemia. Chemical burns meet the burn center criteria.

Chemical in the eye: irrigate at once and at length, and continue in the red eye pathway (pw_eye), which sets the end point of irrigation and calls ophthalmology. Skin burns are washed and sized as in this pathway, and chemical burns meet the burn center criteria.

nodes.ask: Thermal burn, airway safe or secured. First aid, given the time since the burn?
options: Under 3 hours old: cool water 20 minutes, limited in large burns; older: cover
Ice packs for 20 minutes to draw the heat out faster and ease the pain
Silver sulfadiazine cream now, so the wound is covered before transfer
Cool water if the burn happened in the last few minutes, then a dry sheet over it
nodes.chainStep: Within 3 hours: cool water (12 to 25 °C, 53.6 to 77 °F) for 20 minutes, running on the limbs, wet cold compresses on the head, face, trunk and groin; limited in large burns, small children, the frail and shock, keeping the patient warm; after 3 hours, cover without cooling; no ice; cling film or a clean nonadherent dressing; no creams before transfer
nodes.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes gives the most benefit and still helps up to 3 hours after the burn: it eases pain and reduces the need for grafting. Ice is harmful: it deepens the injury through prolonged vasoconstriction. Large burns, infants, older and frail patients and those in shock lose heat fast, so cooling is done with care and the patient is kept warm. Afterwards the wound is covered with cling film or a clean nonadherent dressing; creams and ointments are left off before transfer, so the burn center can assess the wound.

orders.dose: Cool running water (12 to 25 °C, 53.6 to 77 °F) for at least 20 minutes or until the pain is relieved, started as soon as possible and no later than 3 hours after the burn; running water on the limbs, alternating wet cold compresses on the head, face, trunk and groin
20 minutes (the Burns Trauma consensus, the SAFP review, the Australian and New Zealand first aid guidance) against 3 to 5 minutes (StatPearls acute thermal burn chapter, patient advice)
orders.note: The StatPearls patient advice is far shorter than the consensus and reviews; the key follows 20 minutes.

orders.dose: No ice: it deepens the injury and risks hypothermia

sources.where: First aid: what not to do

orders.dose: Care with large burns, infants and children, older or frail patients, shock and cold conditions; avoid prolonged cooling and keep the patient warm; the evidence for 20 minutes of running water comes mostly from burns under 20% TBSA

sources.where: First aid: what not to do

orders.dose: Cling film or a clean nonadherent dressing after cooling; no topical creams or ointments if transferring

nodes.ask: First aid done. Sizing the burn, which skin counts?
options: Partial- and full-thickness skin, by the rule of nines, or Lund-Browder in a child
Each red area, superficial burns included, since the epidermis there is damaged too
The adult rule of nines in a toddler too, with the head counted as 9%
Full-thickness areas, as partial-thickness skin heals by itself
nodes.chainStep: Map depth (superficial, partial, full thickness); count partial- and full-thickness areas only: rule of nines in adults, Lund-Browder chart in children, the patient's palm with fingers for small or scattered burns; weigh the patient; reexamine in the following days
nodes.why: Only partial- and full-thickness burns count toward the TBSA; superficial burns are left out. The adult rule of nines gives the head 9%, each arm 9%, the front and back of the trunk 18% each, each leg 18% and the groin 1%. Children have proportionately larger heads (a young child's head can be 19% of TBSA), so the Lund-Browder chart, which adjusts for age, is more accurate. For small or scattered burns, the patient's palm with the fingers is about 1%, although it overestimates. Partial-thickness burns count because they disrupt the skin's barrier, temperature control and fluid control.

orders.dose: Head 9%, each arm 9%, front of the trunk 18%, back of the trunk 18%, each leg 18%, groin 1%
Lund-Browder chart; a young child's head can be 19% of TBSA, against 9% in an adult
The patient's palm with fingers is about 1% TBSA; it overestimates by 10 to 20%

Superficial: red, dry, painful, blanching, no blisters. Superficial partial: blisters, a moist pink base that blanches, very painful. Deep partial: mottled or white, sluggish or no blanching, less pain. Full thickness: leathery, dry, no blanching, no pain
Burns evolve: reexamine extent and depth over the following days

Child, pattern suggests abuse; immersion lines, cigarette marks, or an unsuitable story
Small partial thickness; under 10% TBSA, thermal, no special site, smoke, full thickness or comorbidity, story fits
Burn center criterion, no formal fluids; 10% TBSA or more but not a major burn, or smaller with full thickness, a special site, a chemical, smoke or comorbidity; story fits

outcomes.if: Major burn, adult; partial and full thickness over 20% TBSA
Major burn, child; partial and full thickness over 10% TBSA, story fits

nodes.summary: Superficial burn only: it is not counted in the TBSA and needs no referral for its size. Over-the-counter analgesia and a soothing topical such as aloe vera; it heals without scarring within 5 to 10 days.

nodes.ask: Partial-thickness burn under 10% TBSA, no special site, story fits. Care?
options: Clean it, dress it, oral analgesia, tetanus by history, and a wound check in days
Oral antibiotics for a week to keep the burn from becoming infected
Admit for Parkland fluids over 24 hours, since the whole burn is partial thickness
Leave it open to the air without a dressing, so the blisters dry out
nodes.chainStep: Clean the burn; topical antibiotic ointment under an absorbent dressing changed once or twice a day, or an occlusive burn dressing left about a week; oral analgesia; tetanus by history; recheck every 2 to 4 days until healing
nodes.why: Small partial-thickness burns are managed as outpatients: cleansing, a topical antibiotic ointment with an absorbent dressing changed once or twice a day or an occlusive burn dressing left about a week, pain relief, and a tetanus booster if needed, since burns are tetanus-prone. Burns evolve, so the wound is reexamined within days. Prophylactic antibiotics are not given; good cleaning and dressings prevent infection. Formal fluids start above 20% TBSA in adults, and patients with small burns who can eat and drink need none.

orders.dose: Clean, then a topical antibiotic ointment under an absorbent dressing changed once or twice a day, or an occlusive burn dressing left about one week; silver sulfadiazine is falling out of favor as it can delay healing

Keep intact blisters during early first aid (Burns Trauma consensus, recommendation 7); remove broken, large, thin-walled or contaminated ones (recommendation 18); debride large, tense or joint-crossing blisters and leave small or palm and sole blisters (StatPearls thermal burns); remove all blisters larger than a thumbnail to judge the depth (SAFP review)
orders.note: The sources disagree on blister care.

orders.dose: Burns are tetanus-prone wounds: a tetanus toxoid vaccine if more than 5 years since the last dose; vaccine plus human tetanus immune globulin if fewer than 3 doses or unknown

sources.where: Tetanus Prophylaxis for Wound Management Recommendations

orders.dose: HyperTET 250 units deep IM, with Td in a different limb and syringe (age 7 and over); under 7, 4.0 units/kg or the whole 250 units
Not given; infection is prevented by cleaning the wound and dressing it
Every 2 to 4 days until signs of healing; reassess extent and depth

nodes.summary: Minor burn: outpatient care with cleaning, a dressing, oral analgesia and tetanus cover, rechecked every few days because burns evolve in depth and extent. No prophylactic antibiotics. A burn that deepens or spreads is measured again against the burn center criteria.

nodes.ask: Meets a burn center criterion, no formal fluids needed. Next?
options: Call the burn center for transfer or advice; analgesia, tetanus and a clean cover
Dress it here and book a clinic visit in a week, since the burn is small
Start Parkland fluids now, since a referral criterion means a formal resuscitation
Prophylactic IV antibiotics while the transfer is being arranged
nodes.chainStep: Discuss with the burn center for transfer or advice; clean and cover without creams; analgesia; tetanus by history; watch circumferential burns and the airway while waiting
nodes.why: The burn center criteria include partial-thickness or deeper burns of 10% TBSA or more; burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum or major joints; full-thickness burns of any size; chemical and electrical burns; inhalation injury; burns with trauma; significant medical problems; special social or rehabilitation needs; and children where the hospital lacks pediatric burn care. Over 50 with more than 10% TBSA is also a referral. Size alone does not decide: a small burn of the hand or face still goes to the burn center. Formal fluids are for burns over 20% TBSA in adults, and antibiotics are not given as prophylaxis. For transfer the burn is cleaned and covered without creams, and the burn center is asked for instructions.

orders.dose: Partial thickness or deeper 10% TBSA or more; face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum or major joints; full thickness of any size; chemical, electrical or inhalation injury; concomitant trauma; medical problems that affect mortality; special social or rehabilitation needs; children where pediatric burn care is lacking
Over 50 with more than 10% TBSA: refer to a burn center
Not read: ameriburn.org terms bar copying; these criteria follow the StatPearls summaries of the ABA list
Clean and cover without topical creams or ointments; call the burn center for instructions
IV morphine, starting 2 to 10 mg per 70 kg and titrated to the lowest effective dose; IV pain medication in a severe burn
Pediatric opioid doses are not in the open sources read
Burns are tetanus-prone wounds: a tetanus toxoid vaccine if more than 5 years since the last dose; vaccine plus human tetanus immune globulin if fewer than 3 doses or unknown

sources.where: Tetanus Prophylaxis for Wound Management Recommendations

orders.dose: Watch any circumferential partial- or full-thickness burn for compartment syndrome

nodes.summary: Burn meeting a burn center criterion without formal fluids: discuss with the burn center for transfer or advice, clean and cover the wound without creams, give analgesia and tetanus cover, and watch circumferential burns and the airway while waiting.

nodes.ask: Adult, partial and full thickness over 20% TBSA. Fluids?
options: Lactated Ringer's at 2 to 4 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 h, half by 8 h after the burn
Normal saline boluses of a liter each until the pulse and the pressure settle down
Lactated Ringer's by Parkland, half over the 8 hours after arrival here
Albumin as the main fluid from the first hour, to hold fluid in the vessels
nodes.chainStep: Lactated Ringer's by weight and burn size: Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 hours, or modified Brooke 2 mL/kg/%TBSA; half in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn, minus fluid already given, the rest over 16 hours; urinary catheter; titrate hourly to a urine output of 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h; no boluses without hypovolemia; document fluids and urine hourly
nodes.why: Formal resuscitation is for partial- and full-thickness burns over 20% TBSA in adults. Lactated Ringer's is the fluid: large volumes of normal saline cause a hyperchloremic acidosis, and boluses without hypovolemia only worsen the edema. The Parkland formula gives 4 mL/kg/%TBSA over the first 24 hours and the modified Brooke 2 mL/kg/%TBSA; either way half goes in over the first 8 hours, counted from the time of the burn and not from arrival, with fluid given before arrival subtracted. One source advises no colloid in the first 8 hours, while the ABA suggests albumin as rescue when crystalloid needs climb. A urinary catheter goes in, because the formula only sets the starting rate and the urine output guides the rest.

Lactated Ringer's is used at every age, and maintenance fluid with dextrose goes on top of the burn formula, because small glycogen stores put children, and infants most, at risk of hypoglycemia; the glucose is checked closely. The Parkland volume for children is 3 mL/kg/%TBSA in two StatPearls chapters and 4 mL/kg/%TBSA in a pediatric table. The urine target is 1 mL/kg/h under 30 kg. Saline boluses add chloride and edema without meeting the ongoing losses.

The formula is only an estimate, and the rate is reassessed every hour. Mannitol is no more effective than fluid loading. If the volume climbs far past the formula and the urine stays low, abdominal compartment syndrome (oliguria with rising airway pressures and falling tidal volumes) is the trap, because more fluid makes it worse.

nodes.ask: Circumferential full-thickness limb burn; distal limb cool, Doppler signal fading. Next?
options: Escharotomy through the eschar along the mid-medial and mid-lateral lines
A formal fasciotomy through the deep fascia as the first decompression step
Elevate the limb and recheck it in 4 hours before cutting

nodes.chainStep: Bedside escharotomy under local anesthetic at the margins: longitudinal mid-medial and mid-lateral incisions through the eschar to fat, stopping above the fascia, unburned skin to unburned skin, sparing the ulnar and common peroneal nerves; then elevation and serial neurovascular checks
nodes.why: A circumferential full-thickness eschar acts as a tourniquet as edema builds under it during resuscitation. Pain out of proportion, pallor, paresthesia, coolness, fading Doppler signals, compartment pressures over 30 mm Hg or a limb saturation under 95% call for escharotomy; pulselessness is a late sign, and elevation alone must not delay it. Escharotomy cuts the eschar but not the deep fascia; fasciotomy is for deep compartments that stay tight afterwards. Cutting the fluids trades the limb for under-resuscitation.

nodes.why: A rigid full-thickness eschar on the chest or abdominal wall can stop the chest from expanding, and escharotomy is indicated when it limits ventilation, even if the burn is not fully circumferential. The breastplate pattern joins bilateral anterior axillary line incisions with transverse cuts across the upper chest and below the costal margins. With equal breath sounds, the stiff eschar rather than a tension pneumothorax explains the pressures. Infants breathe with the abdomen, so abdominal wall burns matter early in them. Extra fluid worsens the edema under the eschar.

nodes.chainStep: Treat the burn by its size and site; report to child protective services; keep the child in a safe place until CPS decides; imaging for occult fractures, which guidelines recommend for non-orthopedic injuries concerning for abuse; document the account, the findings and photographs
nodes.why: Immersion scalds with sharp borders on the buttocks, perineum and legs, in a glove or stocking pattern or symmetric; burns in the shape of an implement such as a cigarette or iron; burns on areas unlikely to touch a hot object by accident; a child who is not independently mobile; and an absent or unsuitable explanation all raise suspicion of maltreatment. Splash burns on exposed areas are more often accidental. The clinician is a mandated reporter: concern, not proof, triggers the report, and child protective services decide whether the child can go home and assess the siblings. The burn is still treated by its size and site.

calculators.note: For a patient seen within 8 hours of the burn; later, use the next calculator. Lactated Ringer's. The clock starts at the burn, not at arrival, and fluid given before arrival comes off the first half. A starting rate only: titrate to urine output, recorded hourly. Children get maintenance fluid with dextrose on top; the sources give them 3 or 4 mL/kg/%TBSA.

calculators.title: Burn fluids, seen 8 or more hours after the burn

outputs.label: Due by now on the schedule
outputs.expr: ml * wt * tbsa / 2 + (h - 8) * ml * wt * tbsa / 2 / 16

outputs.label: Behind the schedule by
outputs.expr: max(0, ml * wt * tbsa / 2 + (h - 8) * ml * wt * tbsa / 2 / 16 - given)

bands.text: On schedule: set the rate by urine output
Behind: a delayed start may need a faster rate and raises fluid needs; set it by urine output, not a bolus
A starting rate, not a bolus: titrate to urine output hourly

sources.where: Fluid resuscitation and early enteral feeding

calculators.note: The 24 hours still count from the burn, and fluid already given counts against them. The schedule runs the second half evenly over hours 8 to 24; the sources set no catch-up rate for a missed first half. After 24 hours the formula gives way to maintenance fluid.

calculators.title: Urine output

bands.text: Under 0.5: below target; raise the rate, no bolus
Over 1: above target; lower the rate
Under 1: below target; raise the rate
Over 1.5: above target; lower the rate

calculators.note: Read the line for your patient. In an adult the target is about 30 to 50 mL/h. The targets for children vary slightly by source.
